messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Kiet had always taken pride in his work as a hotel manager. He was meticulous about every detail, from the cleanliness of the rooms to the politeness of the staff. But everything changed after the toxic chemical exposure incident at the hotel's maintenance facility two years ago. Kiet was nearby when the accident occurred and was exposed to the noxious fumes for several minutes before he could escape. As he recounts that day, his eyes scan the surroundings, a habit he has developed since then - constantly checking for signs of threat or danger. His body tenses up as he remembers the taste of the chemicals burning his throat and lungs. "It's like I'm back there," he says, his voice shaking slightly. "I can still smell it, still feel the panic rising up." After that day, Kiet became increasingly preoccupied with thoughts of helplessness - the feeling that he couldn't stop bad things from happening to him or those around him. He began to question whether his body was reliable anymore, whether it could withstand another assault like that. These fears led him to develop a range of maladaptive strategies: constantly monitoring his body for signs of danger or injury, avoiding reminders of the event by shutting down conversations with colleagues who wanted to discuss it, and scanning his environment obsessively for potential threats. But these attempts at control only seemed to feed back into his cycle of fear. His negative appraisals - that he was helpless, that his body was untrustworthy - made him more prone to false alarms, where he would react as if in danger even when nothing was wrong. A delay in the elevator's arrival or a slight noise in the hallway could send his heart racing and his mind spinning into worst-case scenarios. These episodes of heightened threat perception only served to strengthen Kiet's negative appraisals - reinforcing his conviction that he didn't belong anywhere, that he couldn't trust himself or his surroundings. And these fears, in turn, made it more likely for the traumatic memory to resurface unbidden - with its vivid taste and sense of reliving the event all over again. As Kiet describes this cycle, his eyes darting back and forth, checking the room as if searching for an escape route, it becomes clear that he has become trapped in a self-reinforcing loop. His maladaptive strategies - intended to mitigate the threat - have become the very source of his continued distress. The memories haunt him still, but now they are interwoven with a pervasive sense of danger and distrust. What finally brought Kiet to seek help was the toll this cycle had taken on his relationship with his partner, who could no longer bear the constant tension and hypervigilance that had become his default state. "I just want to be able to relax in my own home," he says, his voice barely above a whisper. But as he looks around the therapist's office, checking for potential threats even here, it is clear that this will be no easy task.
